{"query": "oobleck shear thickening impact paper dynamic jamming front solidification Waitukaitis Jaeger", "results": [{"tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01DFuFPtPFrRWhuBsv52QJHb", "content": [{"title": "messy experiment cleans up physics mystery of cornstarch", "url": "https://www.rdworldonline.com/messy-experiment-cleans-up-physics-mystery-of-cornstarch/"}, {"title": "Messy experiment cleans up physics mystery of cornstarch", "url": "https://news.uchicago.edu/article/2012/07/12/messy-experiment-cleans-physics-mystery-cornstarch"}, {"title": "Ivo 2d impact", "url": "https://jfi.uchicago.edu/~jaeger/group/JaegerGroupPapers/suspensions/Ivo_2d-impact.pdf"}, {"title": "Messy experiment cleans up physics mystery of cornstarch", "url": "https://news.uchicago.edu/story/messy-experiment-cleans-physics-mystery-cornstarch"}, {"title": "Impact-activated solidification of dense suspensions via dynamic jamming fronts", "url": "https://www.ph.ed.ac.uk/events/2014/74304-impact-activated-solidification-of-dense-suspensions-via-dynamic-jamming-fronts"}, {"title": "pubs.rsc.org", "url": "https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/getauthorversionpdf/C4SM00864B"}, {"title": "Team Second", "url": "https://www.flowvis.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Team_Second.pdf"}, {"title": "Impact-activated solidification of dense suspensions via dynamic jamming fronts", "url": "https://research-explorer.ista.ac.at/record/113"}, {"title": "Dynamic Shear Jamming", "url": "https://jfi.uchicago.edu/~jaeger/group/Dense_Suspensions/Projects/Entries/2015/11/25_Dynamic_Shear_Jamming.html"}]}, "The 2012 Nature paper by Waitukaitis and Jaeger is the source for the "dynamic jamming front" idea. Its abstract reports that these stresses originate from an impact-generated solidification front that transforms an initially compressible particle matrix into a rapidly growing jammed region. The authors used high-speed videography, embedded force sensing and X-ray imaging to watch a metal rod hit a cornstarch-in-water suspension. They also developed a model for the dynamic solidification that reproduces the observed behaviour quantitatively.

The paper argues against a simpler explanation. A later Jaeger-group paper says it is not shear thickening per se that accounts for the strong force response, but rather the formation of a dynamic jamming front. The abstract makes a similar point, saying prior interpretations of the impact resistance as dominated by shear thickening need to be revisited.

The group's own description of the process is a snowplow. A solid-like column grows below the impact site, and the way it grows is similar to how a snowplow works. The solidification is temporary. Impacts typically are destructive processes but in the suspension they actually lead to the creation of a solid from a liquid, although only temporarily.

A 2015 Jaeger-group page frames the broader picture. It notes that while shear thickening occurs in the steady state, impact-induced solidification is transient.

I didn't find the full text of the paper itself in these results, only the abstract and press coverage, so the detailed model and data would need to be checked in the Nature article (doi 10.1038/nature11187)."], "durationSeconds": 9.076434557, "searchCount": 1}

{"query": "bats echolocation sonar beam aiming sharpen focus paper Ghose Moss finding", "results": [{"tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01Y17MFQr96vXRrhk7Rt1T4J", "content": [{"title": "pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3384009"}, {"title": "Moss, Ghose research published, featured in media outlets", "url": "https://isr.umd.edu/news/story/moss-ghose--research-published-featured-in-media-outlets"}, {"title": "News Story", "url": "https://isr.umd.edu/news/news_story.php?id=842"}, {"title": "par.nsf.gov", "url": "https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10440552"}, {"title": "Sonar Beam Direction and Flight Control in an Echolocating Bat", "url": "https://drum.lib.umd.edu/handle/1903/3397"}, {"title": "pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3620330"}, {"title": "umi umd 3209", "url": "https://drum.lib.umd.edu/bitstream/1903/3397/1/umi-umd-3209.pdf"}, {"title": "pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov", "url": "https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3437256"}, {"title": "Sonar Beam Direction and Flight Control in an Echolocating Bat", "url": "https://drum.lib.umd.edu/items/52aac432-9a45-4558-86e6-84897aa21550/full"}, {"title": "redesign.bigthink.com", "url": "https://redesign.bigthink.com/?p=32217"}]}, "The search turned up the Ghose and Moss work on sonar beam aiming, though not a single paper matching the exact query.

- **Beam tracking (2003):** In a study of big brown bats (*Eptesicus fuscus*) chasing tethered insects, the bat centers its beam axis on the selected target with a standard deviation (σ) of 3°. The authors concluded that the axis of the bat sonar beam is a good index of selective tracking of targets and in this respect is analogous to gaze in predominantly visual animals.
- **Search versus attack:** A news release from the University of Maryland describes a Journal of Neuroscience article by Moss and Ghose. It reports that bats direct their beams of sound ahead of their flight, like a flashlight. It adds that by adjusting how sharply it follows its beam, the bat is able to adapt between "looking around" in a search mode and "homing in" in attack mode. This is the closest match to your "sharpen focus" wording.
- **Flight control (2006 dissertation):** Ghose's dissertation, with Moss and Timothy Horiuchi, reports that the bat locks its sonar beam tightly onto a target during pursuit. It also describes a coupling between acoustic gaze (sonar beam axis) direction and flight turn rate that can be expressed as a delayed linear control law.
- **Related work:** A separate study of pipistrelle bats in the field found that echolocating bats use a "saccade and fixate" strategy similar to vision. A Science paper with Moss as a coauthor found that Egyptian fruit bats point their sonar sound beam to either side of the target instead. The authors suggest this optimizes the bats' ability to pinpoint the location of a target, but also makes it harder for them to detect a target in the first place.

I did not find the Journal of Neuroscience article itself, so its exact title and year are unconfirmed. The 2003 paper and the dissertation are the most direct matches for the Ghose and Moss findings."], "durationSeconds": 8.681865485000001, "searchCount": 1}

{"query": "Portal gel Repulsion gel Propulsion gel mechanic how it works", "results": [{"tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_016NpY15NmB7zmvomLkhcuon", "content": [{"title": "Repulsion Gel", "url": "https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/Repulsion_Gel"}, {"title": "Gel (Portal 2)", "url": "https://developer.valvesoftware.com/wiki/Repulsion_gel"}, {"title": "Toggle menu", "url": "https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/Blue_Gel"}, {"title": "combineoverwiki.net", "url": "https://combineoverwiki.net/wiki/Propulsion"}, {"title": "Portal 2 Chapter 7 Enrichment Sphere 5", "url": "https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/Portal_2_Chamber_-_Propulsion_Intro"}, {"title": "Repulsion Gel", "url": "https://www.combineoverwiki.net/wiki/Repulsion"}, {"title": "Portal 2 Chapter 7 Enrichment Sphere 5", "url": "https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/Portal_2_Chapter_7_Enrichment_Sphere_5"}, {"title": "Portal Stories: Mel Past Power", "url": "https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/Portal_Stories:_Mel_Past_Power"}, {"title": "modrinth.com", "url": "https://modrinth.com/project/47fKoPi5"}]}, "Repulsion and Propulsion gels are both in-game "mobility gels" in Portal 2. Repulsion gel makes surfaces bouncy, and Propulsion gel makes things move faster.

**Repulsion gel (blue):** It makes objects and players bounce off coated surfaces. Jumping off such a surface launches the player higher than a normal jump, and the height of the jump is proportional to the distance a player falls before rebounding from the Gel. Coated parallel walls let a player ricochet back and forth across the gap. Covered objects, such as turrets, bounce erratically. It is possible to cover Aperture Science Sentry Turrets with the gel, causing them to bounce around, effectively deactivating them.

**Propulsion gel (orange):** Its effect is a reduction in friction. Propulsion gel: Orange, and reduces friction, making objects slippery and players move quickly. In the game's own description, it accelerates the velocity of any object it touches, giving them largely increased speed capabilities and allowing them to vault over pits or reach the far end of a long expanse quickly enough to best a ticking clock.

**Combining them:** When used in combination of Propulsion Gel, the player can travel a considerable distance, which is vital in situations in which Portals cannot be used.

**Portals and placement:** Both gels are applied through the gel droppers and can be redirected with portals. Portals can also be shot under Repulsion Gel vents, allowing the gel to be sent in any area of a Test Chamber.

**Sources:** The Portal Wiki and the Valve Developer Community are the most reliable here. The Combine Overwiki entries contain in-universe lore (for example, the gels' origins as diet products), so treat those origin stories as fiction. The Minecraft Paint Gun mod result is a fan mod, not the original game."], "durationSeconds": 8.483543694, "searchCount": 1}

{"query": "Venus flytrap action potentials counts touches memory Böhm Hedrich paper", "results": [{"tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01Np8n34iM9d7t76hp7URgHj", "content": [{"title": "how the venus flytrap counts 1", "url": "https://www.biologie.uni-wuerzburg.de/en/aktuelles/detail/news/how-the-venus-flytrap-counts-1"}, {"title": "how the venus flytrap counts 1", "url": "https://www.biozentrum.uni-wuerzburg.de/en/news/archive/news-single/news/how-the-venus-flytrap-counts-1/"}, {"title": "How the Venus Flytrap Counts", "url": "https://innovations-report.com/?p=335367"}, {"title": "how the venus flytrap counts 1", "url": "https://www.biozentrum.uni-wuerzburg.de/en/news/news-single/news/how-the-venus-flytrap-counts-1"}, {"title": "Deutsch Intern", "url": "https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/en/news-and-events/news/detail/news/how-the-venus-flytrap-counts"}, {"title": "How the Venus Flytrap Counts", "url": "https://innovations-report.com/life-sciences/how-the-venus-flytrap-counts"}, {"title": "idw – Informationsdienst Wissenschaft", "url": "https://idw-online.de/de/news788672"}, {"title": "Ion channels, excitability, and memory: lessons learnt from the Venus flytrap", "url": "https://scmb.uq.edu.au/node/13322"}, {"title": "Ion channels, excitability, and memory: lessons learnt from the Venus flytrap", "url": "https://scmb.uq.edu.au/event/session/13322"}]}, "The search didn't surface the Böhm-authored paper itself. It returned university press releases and a seminar abstract by Hedrich, which describe the work of Hedrich's group.

- **Memory and counting:** A 2020 study in *Nature Plants*, led by Hasebe's lab with Hedrich's team, found that the trap's short-term memory and the ability to count to two are based on the calcium clock, according to Hedrich. A single touch produces an action potential, and calcium only crosses the closure threshold when two action potentials are triggered in quick succession.
- **Time window:** The press releases give 30 seconds. A Hedrich seminar abstract gives a shorter window: the first action potential is memorized by the trap for 20 sec, and another touch within 20 sec triggers the second, which shuts the trap in a fraction of a second. The two figures conflict, and I can't tell from these results which is correct for a given experiment.
- **Beyond two:** Counting continues past two. Later action potentials increase biosynthesis of the plant hormone jasmonate, and from the fifth electrical excitation on, the plant produces digestive enzymes.
- **Earlier work:** The group's 2016 finding that the plant can count to five is mentioned, but no citation details for that paper came back.
- **Anaesthesia:** A separate *Scientific Reports* study found that the trap cannot "remember" touches during anaesthesia."], "durationSeconds": 10.967465714999998, "searchCount": 1}

{"query": "tardigrade Dsup damage suppressor protein protects DNA radiation paper Hashimoto 2016", "results": [{"tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01EGpgpg7VQwX6UJLb9b8kxz", "content": [{"title": "a 00518", "url": "https://www.u-tokyo.ac.jp/focus/en/articles/a_00518.html"}, {"title": "tardigrade radiation protection gene discovered", "url": "https://astrobiology.com/2016/09/22/tardigrade-radiation-protection-gene-discovered/"}, {"title": "Published by the Students of Johns Hopkins since 1896", "url": "https://www.jhunewsletter.com/article/2016/10/genes-help-water-bears-survive-harsh-conditions"}, {"title": "Published by the Students of Johns Hopkins since 1896", "url": "https://jhunewsletter.com/2016/10/06/genes-help-water-bears-survive-harsh-conditions"}, {"title": "scientists just figured out how tardigrades survive x ray bombardment", "url": "https://www.sciencealert.com/scientists-just-figured-out-how-tardigrades-survive-x-ray-bombardment"}, {"title": "This Protein From Micro-animal Shields DNA From Lethal Radiation", "url": "https://www.asianscientist.com/2016/09/in-the-lab/tardigrade-damage-suppressor-dsup-protein-radiation-damage/"}, {"title": "Extremeophiles and Extreme Environments", "url": "https://astrobiology.com/2016/09/tardigrade-radiation-protection-gene-discovered.html"}, {"title": "Nature Communications (Sep 2016)", "url": "https://doaj.org/article/29c031cfa4904104a798649f99ba60cf"}, {"title": "SEP 20, 2016 12:06 PM PDT", "url": "https://blog.labroots.com/trending/cell-and-molecular-biology/4125/dna-shielded-x-rays-water-bear-protein"}, {"title": "Contact Us marketing@medicilon.com", "url": "https://medicilon.com/press-events/2016928103935-2"}]}, "The 2016 paper is Hashimoto et al., published in Nature Communications under the title "Extremotolerant tardigrade genome and improved radiotolerance of human cultured cells by tardigrade-unique protein" (Nature Communications (Sep 2016)).

- **Source organism:** The team sequenced the genome of Ramazzottius varieornatus, a tardigrade known to survive exposure to high doses of radiation.
- **Main finding:** They identified Dsup, which in human cultured cells roughly halved X-ray-induced DNA damage. The Dsup-expressing cells also kept dividing (approximately half the DNA damage... still capable of reproducing.)
- **Quantified damage:** A Johns Hopkins student newspaper reported that Dsup-expressing cells had about 16% of direct-absorption single-strand breaks versus 33% in controls, and about 18% of reactive-oxygen-species breaks versus 71% in controls. It also reported a 40% reduction in X-ray double-strand breaks (Irradiated Dsup-expressing cells had only 16 percent of the DNA SSBs... Dsup proteins also reduced X-ray induced DSBs by 40 percent.). I could not confirm these exact figures against the paper itself, so treat them as secondary.
- **Proposed mechanism:** The researchers suggest that Dsup's high basicity, especially in its C-terminal region, lets it wrap DNA through electrostatic interactions, shielding it from radiation. This is an inference, not a directly demonstrated mechanism (The researchers infer that Dsup protein's high basicity, particularly in the C-terminal region, is responsible for enclosing the DNA through electrostatic interactions.).
- **Significance:** The authors argued that Dsup works by reducing damage in the first place rather than by repairing it afterward, a departure from the idea that DNA repair mainly explains radiation tolerance (Dsup works to minimize the harm inflicted on the DNA).

A later UC San Diego study examined Dsup's molecular function and offered a molecular explanation for its X-ray protection (scientists at the University of California, San Diego, who analysed Dsup to ascertain its molecular functions.). I did not retrieve details of that work."], "durationSeconds": 8.919442822, "searchCount": 1}

Pair 1: oobleck dynamic jamming front / Elden Ring Bloodhound's Step
PAPER: Waitukaitis & Jaeger, "Impact-activated solidification of dense suspensions via dynamic jamming fronts", Nature 2012 (doi 10.1038/nature11187). Metal rod hits cornstarch-water; high-speed video, embedded force sensors, X-ray imaging. Finding: the huge impact resistance is NOT ordinary shear thickening; the impact creates a growing solid-like jammed region below the rod, a front that advances like a snowplow, compacting particles until it hits the container bottom/ rod stops. Solid is transient: liquid becomes solid only while being hit, then relaxes. Mechanism: particles in the front are compressed into jamming; the front grows with impact speed; unjammed liquid ahead is untouched. Hit hard = floor; touch gently = sink.
GAME: Elden Ring (souls-like), Ash of War "Bloodhound's Step": fast long quickstep with brief near-invisibility, ~16 i-frames (~0.53s) first use, 14 on follow-ups; steer with stick, circles locked-on target to flank/back; costs 5 FP, falls back to normal quickstep without FP; patch 1.06 nerfed distance/i-frames and made repeated use decay. PAPER: Hedrich group (Würzburg) with Hasebe lab, Nature Plants 2020 (earlier Böhm et al. Current Biology 2016 "Venus flytrap counts to five"). Finding: a single touch of a trigger hair makes an action potential that raises cytosolic calcium but not enough; the trap shuts only if a second action potential arrives within ~20-30 s, i.e. calcium accumulation acts as short-term memory/clock ("counts to two"). Further APs keep counting: from AP 3 on it tightens, from ~5 it triggers digestive enzymes and jasmonate hormone biosynthesis. Anaesthetized traps cannot remember touches. Mechanism: calcium level builds with each spike and decays over time; thresholds on the running count gate different responses (close, then digest). Avoids wasting energy on false alarms (raindrops).
GAME: Resident Evil 4 Remake (survival horror), knife parry: a prompt icon appears over knife when an attack is about to land; press parry (L1/LB) in the window; negates damage, perfect parry stuns enemy for a melee follow-up; works on thrown axes/rocks; each parry costs knife durability (heavy hits like chainsaws cost more; attacking also wears it); broken knife can't parry until Merchant repairs it; can't parry grabs. Fun: risky-reward timing turns a resource-starved player into a confident duelist, and durability makes every parry a spend decision.

name: Pair 3: bat sonar beam gaze / Portal 2 gels

Pair 3: bat sonar beam gaze / Portal 2 gels
PAPER: Ghose & Moss, "The sonar beam pattern of a flying bat as it tracks tethered insects", J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 2003 (and Ghose, Moss, Horiuchi 2006 "Sonar gaze strategies... flight control"). Finding: big brown bats aim the sonar beam axis at the chosen target within ~3 degrees SD, so the beam is "acoustic gaze" like eyes; bats shift between wide search mode and tight attack mode by changing how tightly they follow the beam; beam direction couples to flight turn rate by a delayed linear control law. Related: Egyptian fruit bats deliberately point beam to either side of target (Science, Moss coauthor) to localize better via steepest slope of echo, at cost of detecting. Pipistrelles "saccade and fixate". Mechanism: pointing where the beam's steep edge falls maximizes localization precision; widening/narrowing beam and call rate trades search for precision.
GAME: Portal 2 (physics puzzle), gels: Repulsion (blue) makes surfaces bouncy, bounce height proportional to fall distance, parallel coated walls let you ricochet, coated turrets bounce erratically; Propulsion (orange) cuts friction so objects/player accelerate to speed, vault pits; gels redirected via portals; combine blue+orange for long traverses. Fun: the player paints the physics of the level, falling height becomes stored energy, emergent combos.

Pair 4: tardigrade Dsup / Dishonored Blink
PAPER: Hashimoto et al., "Extremotolerant tardigrade genome and improved radiotolerance of human cultured cells by tardigrade-unique protein", Nature Communications 2016. Sequenced Ramazzottius varieornatus; found Dsup (damage suppressor), a tardigrade-unique protein. Expressed in human cells it cut X-ray-induced DNA damage by roughly half (secondary figures: DSBs down ~40%) and cells kept dividing. Mechanism (inferred): Dsup is highly basic, binds DNA/nucleosomes electrostatically and shields it, preventing damage rather than repairing it afterwards (also scavenging hydroxyl radicals). Prevention beats repair.
GAME: Dishonored (immersive sim), Blink: aim a reticle, teleport ~10 m (rank 1) to ~15 m (rank 2) near-instantly; range is a squashed sphere, longer horizontally than vertically; costs ~20% of mana, which regenerates fast so it is usable indefinitely; Greater Blink adds range; Redirective Blink slows time while aiming; Blink Assault knocks enemies down at the end; Dishonored 2 can blink through glass; used to reach ledges, avoid fall damage, get behind enemies. Fun: lets players solve space their own way, cheap enough to chain; precise aiming and an immediate result.

- **Core model:** Ingber's review of cell tensegrity says cells use tensegrity architecture to structure themselves at the molecular level, and that this structure depends on tensile prestress for stability (enables cells to sense and respond to mechanical signals).
- **Prestress and shape:** The model holds that prestress in the cytoskeleton is critical for cell shape stability. That prestress comes from a force balance among microfilaments, intermediate filaments, microtubules, and external adhesions (the stabilizing tensile prestress results from a complementary force balance between multiple, discrete, molecular support elements).
- **Key experimental test:** A 2001 study, which the CROSBI record lists as PNAS 98(14), used traction force microscopy. It found that microtubules bear compression and account for a significant share of cytoskeletal prestress, and that measured static and dynamic mechanics matched the model's predictions (microtubules bear compression and are responsible for a significant portion of the cytoskeletal prestress that determines cell shape stability). The authors are listed as N. Wang and colleagues.
- **Mechanotransduction link:** Integrins and other surface receptors couple the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix and neighboring cells, so mechanical stress passes through these receptors and can change intracellular biochemistry and gene expression (tensegrity predicts that cells are hard-wired to respond immediately to mechanical stresses transmitted over cell surface receptors).
- **Stiffness:** A review chapter by Mofrad and Kamm notes that a tensegrity structure's stiffness is nearly proportional to the prestress it carries (structural rigidity (stiffness) of the matrix is nearly proportional to the level of the prestress that it supports).

The Ingber reviews are the main sources here, and the 2001 Wang et al. experiment is the key primary result. I did not check whether the search missed a specific Ingber primary paper you had in mind."], "durationSeconds": 9.677437646000005, "searchCount": 1}

Finding: Rule 110, a 1D automaton where each cell looks at itself and 2 neighbours (8-entry lookup table), is Turing complete. Mechanism: on a repeating periodic background, stable "gliders" (particle-like patterns) travel and collide; collisions act like logic/signal operations, so data and computation are encoded in glider streams. Class 4 behaviour: between frozen and chaotic. Game of Life likewise is believed universal (gliders, logic gates) though rigorous proof is less settled. Tiny local rules produce emergent, programmable large-scale structure.
GAME: Thief (stealth), Light Gem: a HUD gem at the bottom of screen brightens/darkens with how lit Garrett is at his position, telling how visible he is to guards; has an audio component (noise). Finding: each bird interacts with a fixed number of neighbours (~6-7), regardless of how far they are, not with all neighbours within a set radius. Mechanism: pre-tensioned network where tension members continuously pull against few compression struts, so local load spreads globally and structure stiffens as it is tightened.

The 1999 Nature paper covered deer and bumblebees.

- **The original claim:** Edwards et al. note that an attempt to demonstrate their existence in a natural biological system presented evidence that wandering albatrosses perform Lévy flights when searching for prey on the ocean surface. The 1999 follow-up concluded that deer (Dama dama) and bumblebees (Bombus terricola) also perform Lévy flights.
- **Edwards et al. 2007 (Nature 449:1044–1048):** The authors analyzed a new, high-resolution data set of wandering albatross flights, and found no evidence for Lévy flights. Instead, the flight times are gamma distributed, with a simple exponential decay for the longest flights. They also found that the extremely long flights essential for demonstrating Lévy flight behaviour actually represented time that the birds spent sitting on their nests. For deer and bumblebees, they developed a likelihood method and used Akaike weights to re-analyze the four original deer and bumblebee data sets, and showed that none of them exhibit evidence of Lévy flights. They also argued that the log-log histogram method originally used to ascertain Lévy flight behaviour is not rigorous and yields misleading results.
- **Rebuttal:** Boyer, Miramontes and Ramos-Fernández (arXiv preprint, "Evidence for biological Lévy flights stands") argue that this re-analysis suffers from a conceptual misunderstanding, and that the new albatross data remain consistent with a biological Lévy flight. Their central point is that exponential tails are actually an essential outcome (although overlooked so far) of Lévy random search theory, since they arise from target detection. This is a preprint, and I didn't find evidence in these results of how it was received.
- **Later commentary:** A Scientist article on the paper reports that data loggers fixed to albatrosses in 1992 incorrectly recorded nest-sitting as food searching time. Edwards's group also presented the same conclusions in a 2007 conference abstract.

The search did not surface the full text of the 1996 or 1999 Viswanathan papers, nor any follow-up literature beyond the rebuttal, so the wider scientific consensus is not established here."], "durationSeconds": 8.39068267000001, "searchCount": 1}

PAPER: Edwards et al., "Revisiting Lévy flight search patterns of wandering albatrosses, bumblebees and deer", Nature 449:1044 (2007). Original claims: Viswanathan et al. 1996 (albatross) and 1999 (deer, bumblebees) said step lengths follow a power-law (Lévy flight), optimal for sparse unpredictable prey: many short local hops with rare very long jumps. Edwards re-analysed with likelihood/Akaike weights: no Lévy flight; albatross flight times are gamma-distributed with exponential tail; the very long "flights" were just time sitting on the nest (loggers recorded nest-sitting as search); log-log histogram method misleading. Rebuttal (Boyer, Miramontes, Ramos-Fernandez): exponential tails are expected in Lévy search theory because target detection truncates steps; evidence stands. Surprising: a famous result was partly a data-logger artefact. Mechanism of the theory: heavy-tailed step lengths revisit sites less, covering sparse space efficiently.

Warzone 2.0 can split the circle into 2-4 smaller circles that later merge, producing micro-battles. PUBG blue zone damage scales with distance outside. Fun: forced convergence creates clashes; rotation timing/risk decisions; split circles add unpredictability.
